title: ECT Is a Controversial Treatment of Last Resort. I Wish I’d Gotten It Sooner
author: Ted Scheinman
body:
Electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, isn’t terribly fashionable. People sometimes get an uneasy look on their faces at the mention of it. The treatment has come a long way since those agonizing scenes in Miloš Forman’s One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest—but I understand why ECT still freaks people out. Electricity is what Victor Frankenstein used to animate his monster; as recently as 2020, the state used it to execute murderers.

Nevertheless, in 2021, I decided to undergo the treatment, allowing an electrical current to induce brain seizures in hopes of relieving my depression, because I had tried everything else and was close to giving up on life completely.

Though I’m not a doctor, I knew the well-documented side effects of ECT; most famously, memory loss. As a writer, a musician, and a nostalgist, I cared deeply about preserving my powers of recollection. But by the time I began getting shocked, the thought of losing a little memory was less scary to me than spending another day getting crushed by this long disease.

ECT is not a one-time thing. My doctors began me on three sessions a week. The treatments always happened early in the mornings. When other people were on their first cup of coffee, I was watching the anesthesiologist plug his tubes into the IV port in my arm. When the sparrows outside were singing, I was lying on a surgical table as the medical team rubbed a conductive glue onto my temples. It felt like warm honey and was meant to help the electricity penetrate my skull.

Then the anesthesiologist would tell me to count backward from 100 as he began the flow of the anesthetic propofol, plus a muscle relaxant, which, between them, would have me laughing and then passing out before I got past 96. I would wake up in a different room nearby, sometimes with a headache, sometimes not, sometimes euphoric, sometimes not. I did this three times in the first week. Each time, I surrendered myself. I tried to have faith, or at least simulate faith, that this odd practice would bring me back to life.

The oddest part was when it began to work.

It took a lot. A lot of ECT. A lot of patience from my girlfriend at the time. A lot of friends taking turns driving me to appointments. A lot of faith in the strange ritual of voluntarily applying electrical currents through my brain. Because I got so many treatments—around two dozen, twice as many as a typical patient—eventually they took a toll, and I found myself unable to summon certain memories from the previous six months, in some cases longer. Yet I emerged from ECT, and from the depression preceding it, much healthier than I’d been in years.

Pretty soon I went from being worried about what I’d lost to being astonished at what I had gained. I could write for an audience again, an ability I’d surrendered to depression long before ECT. I could play music in public again. The crying fits stopped. Some of my lost memories came back. I returned to the world.

Still, people are, understandably, pretty shocked when they hear that I embraced ECT. What surprises them even more: that I really, really wish I’d gotten it sooner.

In modern American psychiatry, ECT is held explicitly as a treatment of last resort, reserved for the stubbornest of what’s called treatment-resistant depression. That wasn’t always the case.

In the earliest days of electroshock, long before muscle relaxants and anesthesia were even in the picture, doctors held ECT as the gold standard, and sometimes as a first-line treatment. Lothar Kalinowsky, a pioneer of ECT in the U.S., said in a 1978 interview that a course of five or six sessions could be effective for depression. As psychopharmacology began to take hold, doctors began prescribing ECT later and later in a given course of depression, if at all, and patients accordingly required longer courses: around eight to ten.

Today, according to Harold Sackeim, a foundational figure in modern neuromodulation, now professor of psychiatry at the Medical University of South Carolina, a typical course consists of 10 to 12 treatments. In part because of how long I’d waited for ECT, my own illness required around twice that number.

In most cases, before recommending ECT these days, a doctor must deem a patient to have exhausted any possibility of improvement from talk therapy and from psychopharmacology. Most patients who reach the point of electrical necessity will have tried not only multiple selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), but also tricyclic and tetracyclic antidepressants and perhaps a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI). That means months and months of spinning from one prescription to another, waiting for relief that too often doesn’t arrive. Meanwhile, a lot of patients don’t even know to ask for ECT, and doctors can be slow to prescribe it.

“What we’ve done is essentially reserve ECT for the more and more resistant patients,” Sackeim tells me.

Since my own treatment, I’ve interviewed neurologists and ECT doctors. Each of them has agreed with my thesis that if I’d gotten ECT sooner, I would’ve spent less time in the depths of unlivable depression—one that had lasted for years.

They also agree that I would almost certainly have experienced less memory loss.

The complicating factor here is that depression itself often hampers memory, and the longer and deeper the depression, the more gaps and blurs a person will experience in their memory, even before receiving ECT.

In other words, getting shocked earlier could have required me to undergo fewer treatments, while potentially preserving more of my memory.

That might sound counterintuitive. But a lot of things about ECT are counterintuitive. For one thing, most people don’t know that ECT consistently spurs measurable growth in one’s hippocampus, a part of the brain that can literally shrink during sustained periods of depression. What’s more, emerging research suggests that ECT stimulates neurogenesis: the production of new neurons and of the glial cells that support them.

Electricity doesn’t merely destroy; it can also create.

ECT isn’t for everybody, and its side effects are real. But I will never stop being grateful for it. Five years have now passed since I last encountered those electrodes. In those five years, I’ve gotten married, written a new book, and lived a happier and fuller life than the one that I had accepted for too much of my adulthood.

The history of ECT is rife with abuses. But what about those of us who could have lived fuller lives, sooner, through the judicious application of some electricity? I hope the next person who could benefit from the treatment won’t have to wait, as I did, until it’s almost too late.
